title: What the Body Remembers
logline: A coach or teacher who once had a violent temper now works patiently with young people, day after day. They still notice the moment before they would once have exploded. They just don't go there anymore.

object.note: Object 3 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From a day where pushed and willing hands move differently to a person who knows in the body what the old heat felt like, and no longer goes there.

thread_out.thread: What replaces the heat is not certainty but something quieter; the next film stays inside that quiet, in a household that cannot settle whether someone should go abroad for work.

requirements: A person locally known for having changed in this way, willing to speak about it on their own terms
A rural school, sports ground or workshop where they currently work with others regularly
Consent from any young people shown, and their guardians where required

lesson.in_simple_terms: Anger never comes with real delight, even when it feels deserved. The texts describe it as burning the person who holds it, and advise living watchfully because it visits ordinary people so often.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: තරහ කොතරම් සාධාරණ යැයි හැඟුණත් එය කිසිදා සතුටක් නොවන බවත්, එය මුලින්ම දවන්නේ තරහ ගන්නා කෙනාම බවත් කියන ධර්මය, ඒ නිසා සිහියෙන් ජීවත් වන්නට උපදෙස් දෙයි.
lesson.the_teaching: Both hate-rooted minds always come with a painful mental feeling and never contain joy (pīti), unlike greed-rooted minds, which can. Pradeepika describes what aversion does to the one who holds it: they cannot see good from bad or right from wrong, and it keeps the mind burning; one of its causes is not thinking the object through. It closes by saying that ordinary people meet these states often, and so should live with mindfulness and wisdom to hold back from them.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film stays with an ordinary day of coaching or teaching, where corrections are given, mistakes repeated and patience tested. The viewer can watch for a small, visible pause where an old reaction once came straight away, and hears the person describe, in their own words, what anger used to feel like and what has changed, as something still being lived rather than a finished story.
lesson.caution: This does not mean anger only hurts the angry person or that past harm to others is erased; the texts are plain that this state also leads to harming others.
lesson.builds_on: Willing Hands showed how being pushed changes the texture of effort; this film turns to a person who no longer follows the push of their own heat, and to what the texts say that heat is like from the inside.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
